To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NK(1)/ NK(2) antagonists are involved in stress-induced colonic motor alterations in gerbils.

NK(1)/ NK(2) antagonists are useful in treating stress-related functional gastrointestinal disorders and that NK(1)-antagonism is slightly more effective in inhibiting stress-induced colonic motor alterations than NK(2)-antagonism.

NK(1)- and NK(2)-receptors are involved in stress related colonic motor alterations as well as visceral pain responses in the gerbil, and that combined antagonists may be more effective in treating visceral pain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the tachykinins and tachykinergic neurons in the control of gastrointestinal motility and the development of functional gastrointestinal disorders.
the role of tachy kinin NK(1)/ NK(2) in colonic sensitivity, visceral pain and stress induced defecation in the gerbils.
the development of novel drugs for the treatment of functional bowel disorders such as Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of tachy-kinin NK(2) and NK(1) receptors in colitis and visceral pain is still not fully elucidated and that further research is needed.
NK1 and NK2 receptors are involved in the modulation of colonic sensitivity in gerbils.

NK(1)- and NK(2)-receptors have a role in mediating visceral pain responses in conscious gerbiles and that combined NK(1)-NK(2)-receptor blockade is a more potent strategy to attenuate visceral pain responses in this species than NK(1)- or NK(2)- receptor blockade alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NK(1)/ NK(2) dual antagonists may provide a better clinical outcome in functional gastrointestinal disorders.
the NK(1) receptor plays a role in both the stress response and visceral hypersensitivity, whereas the NK(2) plays a more prominent role in the stress response.
NK1 and NK2 receptors are involved in the regulation of colonic motor activity and stress-evoked defacation in gerbills, and that combined antagonists may be more effective than single compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NK1 and NK2 receptor antagonists are involved in stress-evoked defacation and colonic pain in gerbils.
gerbils may be a useful species for studying human gastrointestinal disorders.
NK(1)/2 receptor antagonists can be used to treat visceral pain and stress-induced defecalatory disorders.
